title: When, Why, and How CMB Compression Fails

paper.title: When, Why, and How CMB Compression Fails
paper.abstract: Abstract We test when compressed CMB likelihoods can be reliably used to constrain new physics beyond Λ \Lambda CDM, formulating concrete criteria for when , why , and how CMB compression fails. We derive our conclusions by exploring a broad set of models that modify different aspects of the cosmological evolution, including late-time dark-energy dynamics, non-standard late-time dark-matter evolution through interactions or decay, and dark-matter models with persistently non-standard redshift evolution. For each case, we compare the results obtained from data combinations based on the full Planck-CMB likelihood with their counterparts based on a compressed CMB likelihood calibrated in Λ \Lambda CDM. We find that the compression remains accurate for late-time dark-energy extensions that preserve the dark-matter background evolution and do not introduce significant additional perturbative effects. By contrast, modifying the dark-matter evolution breaks the mapping between the present-day matter density and the matter density at the epochs relevant to the CMB, causing the compressed constraints to fail even when the modification acts exclusively at late times. In these cases, the compressed likelihood can drastically alter the geometry of the multidimensional posterior distributions, shifting their centers, producing strongly anisotropic deformations, reordering principal modes, and generating genuine mixing and rotation of their eigendirections. These multidimensional distortions propagate into substantially incorrect marginalized constraints on cosmological parameters, with differences between the full and compressed analyses reaching nearly an order of magnitude in some of the cases studied here.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Over more than two decades, full-sky satellite missions such as WMAP [ 39 , 140 ] and Planck [ 9 , 11 ] , complemented by the higher angular resolution of ground-based experiments such as the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) [ 234 , 202 , 197 ] and the South Pole Telescope (SPT) [ 123 , 56 ] , have established the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation as one of the most powerful and precise probes in modern cosmology. The increasing precision of CMB measurements has progressively tightened constraints on cosmological parameters and models of new physics, while confirming the excellent agreement of the observed anisotropies with the standard Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology [ 11 , 202 , 56 ] . At the same time, however, persistent tensions within Λ \Lambda CDM, including the Hubble tension [ 276 , 93 , 89 , 227 , 249 , 252 , 4 , 96 , 158 , 131 , 144 , 277 , 86 , 104 , 94 , 54 ] and the preference for dynamical dark energy recently emerging from DESI analyses [ 6 , 196 ] , 1 1 1 For a non-exhaustive selection of discussions surrounding this preference, see, e.g. [ 79 , 255 , 199 , 125 , 283 , 307 , 265 , 60 , 224 , 105 , 41 , 29 , 185 , 237 , 127 , 235 , 304 , 154 , 240 , 132 , 126 , 103 , 161 , 241 , 248 , 290 , 247 , 263 , 65 , 66 , 217 , 183 , 174 , 113 , 268 , 260 , 55 , 138 , 67 , 70 , 71 , 72 , 151 , 73 , 133 , 150 , 209 , 297 , 97 , 81 , 160 , 184 , 129 , 182 , 238 , 30 ] . have motivated growing interest in alternative models and physical mechanisms beyond the standard cosmological paradigm. 2 2 2 The significance of the so-called S 8 S_{8} tension [ 92 , 85 , 213 , 23 , 250 , 32 , 31 , 156 , 100 , 2 , 272 , 139 , 82 , 64 , 162 , 111 , 137 , 99 , 1 , 291 , 3 ] is milder and less clear-cut. The KiDS-Legacy reanalysis reported values of S 8 S_{8} in good agreement with Planck [ 291 ] , whereas the Dark Energy Survey Year 6 (DES-Y6) results still find a mild mismatch with CMB constraints at ∼ 2.6 \sim 2.6 – 2.8 ​ σ 2.8\sigma [ 3 ] . Since any such mechanism must preserve the level of agreement with CMB data set by Λ \Lambda CDM, confronting models of new physics with CMB observations is more important and timely than ever. However indispensable in practice, testing models of new physics against CMB data has two important limitations. First, it is computationally expensive and inconvenient for efficient scans across large model spaces. Second, it is not easily applicable to models for which the evolution of linear perturbations is either technically and computationally demanding (as often occurs in modified-gravity theories [ 76 , 166 ] ) or not well defined (as in some purely phenomenological models). These limitations have motivated the development of compression schemes , which summarize the information contained in the full CMB power spectrum in a limited number of parameters [ 101 ] . The most notable example is given by the so-called shift parameters ( ℓ a \ell_{a} , R R ), which were first introduced with the aim of exploring cosmic acceleration and the landscape of dark energy models [ 101 , 286 , 287 ] . R ≡ Ω m ​ H 0 2 ​ D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) R\equiv\sqrt{\Omega_{m}H_{0}^{2}}D_{M}(z_{\star}) represents the scaled angular diameter distance to the last-scattering surface, while ℓ a ≡ π ​ D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) / r s ⋆ \ell_{a}\equiv\pi D_{M}(z_{\star})/r_{s}^{\star} defines the multipole corresponding to the characteristic angular scale subtended by the sound horizon at photon decoupling. In Refs. [ 287 , 288 ] it was subsequently shown that combining the shift parameters with the physical baryon density ω b = Ω b ​ h 2 \omega_{b}=\Omega_{b}h^{2} (and possibly the inflationary spectral index n s n_{s} ) provides a compact summary of the CMB information relevant for cosmological parameter constraints. This set of quantities is commonly referred to as the CMB distance priors . 3 3 3 Other methods to compress CMB information have also been explored. For example, in Ref. [ 233 ] the authors applied the Massively Optimized Parameter Estimation and Data compression to the Planck-2015 temperature likelihood and showed that the standard Λ \Lambda CDM cosmological parameter constraints can be derived from a compressed likelihood of just six Gaussian-distributed data points. More recently, Ref. [ 21 ] explored self-supervised machine-learning techniques for data compression and cosmological inference. Despite being among the least model-dependent quantities that can be extracted from the CMB, the shift parameters are not direct observables. Quantities such as ℓ a \ell_{a} and R R are inferred from the observed temperature and polarization power spectra within a fiducial cosmological model, typically Λ \Lambda CDM [ 287 , 205 , 288 ] . Their values and correlations therefore depend on how the fiducial model relates cosmological parameters to the observed CMB features [ 310 ] . Using the resulting compressed likelihood to constrain a different cosmology implicitly assumes that the relevant CMB physics, and hence this mapping, remains sufficiently unchanged [ 205 , 310 ] . A commonly adopted working criterion is to distinguish between modifications occurring before and after recombination. Late-time models are generally expected to be more reliable in this respect, since they leave the physics responsible for the primary CMB anisotropies essentially unchanged [ 287 , 205 , 310 ] . By contrast, pre-recombination new physics can modify the acoustic physics itself and therefore invalidate a compression calibrated within Λ \Lambda CDM [ 253 , 310 ] . A number of studies have therefore assessed the validity and regime of applicability of compressed CMB information beyond the fiducial Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology. Initial studies tested the robustness of the shift parameters against relatively simple departures from flat Λ \Lambda CDM [ 287 , 205 , 288 ] , while later analyses extended these tests to models involving dynamical dark energy, massive neutrinos, additional relativistic degrees of freedom, spatial curvature, and modifications of the primordial power spectrum [ 310 ] . More recently, the compressed likelihood CMBComp [ 264 ] has addressed this model dependence more systematically by constructing compression schemes tailored to specific classes of cosmological models. 4 4 4 For instance, the ν ​ Λ \nu\Lambda CDM model is described by the four-parameter compression ( ℓ a , R , ω b , ω c ) (\ell_{a},R,\omega_{b},\omega_{c}) , calibrated specifically within the corresponding model space. Our work extends these robustness tests with the broader goal of identifying the physical conditions under which compressed CMB information can be reliably used to test models of new physics. In particular, we investigate which properties of a cosmological model determine whether compressed CMB information remains reliable, focusing on the physical sector affected by the new dynamics and on which pieces of CMB information are consequently modified. To this end, we consider a set of phenomenologically motivated models proposed in connection with concrete challenges to the standard cosmological paradigm and use them as representative test cases to isolate qualitatively different departures from the physics underlying the CMB compression. Taking Λ \Lambda CDM as our benchmark scenario, we first extend it by introducing a constant dark-energy equation of state (EoS) w DE w_{\rm DE} . We then consider the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder (CPL) parametrization of dynamical dark energy [ 68 , 191 ] and a sign-switching cosmological constant [ 20 ] . These three models modify the late-time dark-energy background while leaving the standard scaling of the matter densities unchanged. We then turn to interacting dark-energy (IDE) models, where energy exchange within the dark sector alters the dynamics of both dark energy and dark matter [ 46 , 279 ] , and consequently the relation between the dark-matter abundance constrained by the CMB at recombination and its present-day value. Finally, we consider two complementary scenarios in which the departure from Λ \Lambda CDM is confined to the dark-matter sector: decaying dark matter [ 33 , 230 ] and dark matter with a nonzero EoS [ 165 ] . In the former, the dark-matter evolution is modified predominantly at late times, while in the latter the standard scaling ρ dm ∝ a − 3 \rho_{\rm dm}\propto a^{-3} is modified throughout the cosmological evolution. Together, these models allow us to test whether the validity of the CMB compression depends not simply on when the new physics becomes relevant, but on how it modifies the relation between the dark-matter abundance probed by the CMB and its present-day value. We find a clear qualitative distinction depending on the physical sector affected by the new dynamics. The compression remains remarkably robust for models in which the departure from Λ \Lambda CDM is confined to the late-time dark-energy sector and the standard evolution of the matter densities is preserved. By contrast, when the dark-matter sector acquires a non-standard evolution, the compressed likelihood fails to reproduce the constraints obtained from the full CMB temperature and polarization spectra. In these cases, the compressed likelihood can distort the multidimensional geometry of the posterior distributions, ultimately leading to marginalized constraints that in some cases differ by nearly an order of magnitude from those obtained with the full CMB likelihood. We trace this breakdown primarily to the failure of the usual mapping between the dark-matter abundance constrained by the CMB around recombination and its present-day value. In addition, compressing the full spectra into a small number of background quantities can discard perturbation-level information that becomes relevant when the dark-matter sector is modified. Our results therefore show that the validity of compressed CMB information is determined not simply by when new physics becomes active, but also by which physical sector it affects and whether the relations implicitly assumed by the compression remain valid. The paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II we review the compression scheme adopted in our analysis. In Sec. III we discuss the datasets and methodology used to obtain our results, together with the diagnostic tools developed to perform a detailed comparison of the posterior distributions. In Sec. IV we introduce the models against which we test the CMB compression. We present the results in Sec. V . A critical discussion of our findings and their implications follows in Sec. VI . Finally, we present our conclusions in Sec. VII . Additional tests of the robustness of our main conclusions against different compression choices and dataset combinations are presented in Appendix A .

sections.heading: II CMB compression
sections.text: In this section, we give a brief introduction to the shift parameters ( R , ℓ a ) (R,\ell_{a}) , which together with the physical baryon density ω b \omega_{b} constitute the CMB distance priors. We then describe their relation to the compression scheme adopted in this paper. The first shift parameter, R R , is defined as [ 47 ] R ≡ Ω m ​ H 0 2 ​ D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) , R\equiv\sqrt{\Omega_{m}H_{0}^{2}}\,D_{M}(z_{\star}), (1) where H 0 H_{0} is the Hubble constant, Ω m \Omega_{m} is the present-day matter density parameter, and D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) D_{M}(z_{\star}) is the comoving distance to the last-scattering surface. Throughout this work, we consider a spatially flat, homogeneous and isotropic Universe described by a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric. In this framework, the comoving distance to the last-scattering surface reads D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) = 1 H 0 ​ ∫ 0 z ⋆ d ​ z ′ E ⁡ ( z ′ ) , D_{M}(z_{\star})=\frac{1}{H_{0}}\int_{0}^{z_{\star}}\frac{dz^{\prime}}{E(z^{\prime})}, (2) where E ⁡ ( z ) ≡ H ⁡ ( z ) / H 0 E(z)\equiv H(z)/H_{0} is the dimensionless expansion rate of the Universe, and we work in units where c = 1 c=1 . The redshift z ⋆ z_{\star} denotes photon decoupling and is conventionally identified with the peak of the Thomson-scattering visibility function. Both z ⋆ z_{\star} and D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) D_{M}(z_{\star}) depend on the assumed cosmology and can be computed numerically using Boltzmann solvers such as CAMB [ 178 ] or CLASS [ 175 , 44 ] . Historically, the shift parameter R R was introduced to capture the dominant effect of late-time geometry on the angular structure of the CMB power spectrum. Ref. [ 47 ] showed that models with the same primordial perturbation spectrum and the same physical matter densities at decoupling can produce nearly identical primary CMB spectra when their angular-distance scaling is also preserved. The second shift parameter, ℓ a \ell_{a} , is defined as [ 106 ] ℓ a ≡ π θ s ⋆ , \ell_{a}\equiv\frac{\pi}{\theta_{s}^{\star}}, (3) where θ s ⋆ ≡ r s ⋆ / D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) \theta_{s}^{\star}\equiv r_{s}^{\star}/D_{M}(z_{\star}) is the angular acoustic scale subtended by the comoving sound horizon at photon decoupling, r s ⋆ r_{s}^{\star} . Interestingly, θ s ⋆ \theta_{s}^{\star} is determined by the ratio of two quantities sensitive to different epochs. The comoving distance D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) D_{M}(z_{\star}) depends on the integrated expansion history between the last-scattering surface and today. By contrast, the comoving sound horizon at photon decoupling is determined by the pre-recombination expansion history, r s ⋆ = ∫ z ⋆ ∞ d ​ z ′ ​ c s ​ ( z ′ ) H ⁡ ( z ′ ) , r_{s}^{\star}=\int_{z_{\star}}^{\infty}dz^{\prime}\,\frac{c_{s}(z^{\prime})}{H(z^{\prime})}, (4) where c s ​ ( z ) c_{s}(z) denotes the sound speed of the tightly coupled photon-baryon plasma given by c s ​ ( z ) = 1 3 ​ [ 1 + R b ​ ( z ) ] , R b ​ ( z ) ≡ 3 ​ ω b 4 ​ ω γ ​ 1 1 + z . c_{s}(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3\left[1+R_{b}(z)\right]}},\quad R_{b}(z)\equiv\frac{3\omega_{b}}{4\omega_{\gamma}}\frac{1}{1+z}. (5) Although both r s ⋆ r_{s}^{\star} and D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) D_{M}(z_{\star}) are model dependent, their ratio is exceptionally tightly constrained by the observed acoustic pattern of the CMB. As a result, θ s ⋆ \theta_{s}^{\star} remains remarkably stable across broad classes of models that preserve the underlying acoustic physics, making ℓ a \ell_{a} particularly well suited for CMB compression. The shift parameters R R and ℓ a \ell_{a} capture the dominant geometrical information encoded in the CMB, but an accurate compression must also retain the physical quantities that determine the acoustic structure at recombination. This role is naturally played by the physical baryon density ω b \omega_{b} . Its value directly affects the sound speed of the photon-baryon fluid, the sound horizon, and the relative heights and structure of the acoustic peaks in the CMB spectra. Together, these effects tightly constrain ω b \omega_{b} and generate correlations with the shift parameters that must be preserved in the compression scheme. This leads to the three-parameter distance-prior set ( R , ℓ a , ω b ) (R,\ell_{a},\omega_{b}) considered in Ref. [ 287 ] . 5 5 5 Additional parameters may be required depending on the information included in the analysis. A notable example is the scalar spectral index, n s n_{s} , whose inclusion becomes relevant when using observables sensitive to the shape of the matter power spectrum [ 205 ] . Since in our analysis BAO measurements are used only as geometrical probes, we do not retain n s n_{s} as an additional compression parameter [ 205 ] . In our work, we adopt the compression vector ( 1 / θ s ⋆ , ω m , ω b ) (1/\theta_{s}^{\star},\omega_{m},\omega_{b}) , where ω m = ω c + ω b + ω ν \omega_{m}=\omega_{c}+\omega_{b}+\omega_{\nu} . Our compression vector is closely related to the standard distance-prior set ( R , ℓ a , ω b ) (R,\ell_{a},\omega_{b}) . 6 6 6 Similar parametrizations have been successfully adopted in Refs. [ 189 , 200 , 225 ] . For cosmologies that preserve the standard pre-recombination physics, the two parametrizations are expected to encode equivalent information. For our purposes, however, the adopted parametrization offers a more transparent physical interpretation by separating the geometrical information carried by the angular acoustic scale from that associated with the physical matter densities. Under standard pre-recombination physics and for fixed radiation and neutrino sectors, the sound horizon r s ⋆ r_{s}^{\star} is determined by the physical densities ω m \omega_{m} and ω b \omega_{b} . Once this early-time calibration is specified, 1 / θ s ⋆ = D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) / r s ⋆ 1/\theta_{s}^{\star}=D_{M}(z_{\star})/r_{s}^{\star} isolates the remaining dependence on the distance to the last-scattering surface and hence on the post-recombination expansion history. The vector ( 1 / θ s ⋆ , ω m , ω b ) (1/\theta_{s}^{\star},\omega_{m},\omega_{b}) therefore provides a clean separation between the geometrical information contained in D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) D_{M}(z_{\star}) and the physical densities that determine the acoustic ruler against which this distance is measured. This separation is less explicit in the traditional basis ( R , ℓ a , ω b ) (R,\ell_{a},\omega_{b}) . Indeed, R R combines D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) D_{M}(z_{\star}) with the present-day matter density, while ℓ a \ell_{a} also depends on D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) D_{M}(z_{\star}) through the angular acoustic scale. The two parameters therefore share the same dependence on the distance to last scattering. Replacing R R with ω m \omega_{m} removes this common geometrical dependence and makes the separation between geometry and physical densities explicit. This separation becomes particularly informative when the evolution of the matter sector itself is modified. For completeness, in Appendix A.1 we explicitly verify the equivalence between the two formulations of the CMB distance priors.

sections.heading: III dataset and methodology
sections.text: In this section, we describe the datasets and methodology adopted in our analysis. We first summarize the numerical implementation and statistical framework used for cosmological parameter inference. We then describe the tailored geometric posterior analysis developed to quantify the differences between the full and compressed CMB constraints, together with its numerical implementation.

sections.heading: III.1 Datasets and standard parameter inference
sections.text: We perform a systematic comparison of cosmological constraints obtained using the full and compressed CMB likelihoods across a set of representative models chosen to isolate qualitatively different departures from Λ \Lambda CDM and identify the physical properties that determine the validity of the CMB compression. Theoretical predictions are computed using the Boltzmann solver CLASS [ 44 , 175 ] . We use the standard public implementation for Λ \Lambda CDM and for scenarios already supported by the code, together with dedicated modified versions for the non-standard dark-energy and dark-matter models introduced in Sec. IV . These implementations consistently evolve the background cosmology and, whenever required for the full-CMB analysis, the associated linear perturbations. For each model, we run parallel Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses using Cobaya [ 271 ] . The chains are evolved until convergence according to the Gelman-Rubin criterion [ 124 ] , requiring R − 1 < 0.01 R-1<0.01 , and subsequently post-processed using GetDist [ 179 ] to derive marginalized parameter constraints and posterior distributions. We further analyze the multidimensional geometry of the posterior distributions using the PostModes package described in the following subsection. The full- and compressed-CMB analyses use the same cosmological parameters, prior distributions, and observational datasets. They differ only in the treatment of the CMB information. In one case, we use the full Planck temperature and polarization likelihood, while in the other we replace it with the compressed likelihood introduced in Sec. II . The observational datasets and likelihoods entering these analyses are the following: • Full Planck-CMB : Our full CMB likelihood is based on the Planck 2018 data [ 10 , 11 ] and combines the low- ℓ \ell temperature Commander likelihood, the low- ℓ \ell E-mode polarization SimAll likelihood, and the high- ℓ \ell Plik TT, TE, and EE likelihood [ 10 ] . We do not include the CMB lensing-reconstruction likelihood because our goal is to compare the information encoded in the primary CMB spectra with that retained by their compression. Including lensing reconstruction would add extra late-time information on structure growth that is not encoded in the compressed likelihood. Gravitational-lensing effects on the primary TT, TE, and EE spectra are nevertheless consistently included. • Compressed Planck-CMB : We perform an MCMC analysis of Λ \Lambda CDM using exclusively the Planck 2018 temperature and polarization data listed above. From the resulting MCMC chains, following the parametrization introduced in Sec. II , we extract the posterior mean 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance 𝐂 \mathbf{C} of the three-dimensional compression vector 𝐱 = ( 1 / θ s , ω m , ω b ) \mathbf{x}=(1/\theta_{s},\omega_{m},\omega_{b}) . We then use these quantities to construct a compressed Planck multivariate Gaussian likelihood, 7 7 7 Available at https://github.com/williamgiare/wgcosmo . − 2 ​ ln ⁡ ℒ CMB 3 × 3 = ( 𝐱 − 𝝁 ) T ​ 𝐂 − 1 ​ ( 𝐱 − 𝝁 ) , -2\ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm CMB}^{3\times 3}=\left(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\right)^{\rm T}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\right), (6) which preserves the means, variances, and correlations of these three quantities. • DESI : We use the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) DR2 Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) measurements from galaxies, quasars, and Ly α \alpha -forest data [ 28 , 5 ] in seven redshift bins spanning 0.295 ≤ z eff ≤ 2.330 0.295\leq z_{\rm eff}\leq 2.330 [ 6 ] . The likelihood includes the full covariance matrix of the measurements [ 6 ] . • PantheonPlus : We use Type-Ia Supernovae (SN) distance-modulus measurements from the Pantheon+ sample, consisting of 1701 light curves from 1550 unique spectroscopically classified SN [ 51 ] . Throughout this work, we denote by • A A : the posterior and marginalized constraints obtained from the full Planck-CMB likelihood combined with DESI BAO and PantheonPlus SN; • B B : the posterior and marginalized constraints obtained from the compressed Planck-CMB likelihood combined with DESI BAO and PantheonPlus SN.

sections.heading: III.2 Posterior eigenmode analysis
sections.text: To characterize more systematically the differences between the full and compressed CMB constraints, we complement the standard comparison of marginalized constraints on cosmological parameters with a broader geometric analysis of the corresponding multidimensional posteriors. To this end we develop the PostModes package. 8 8 8 Available at https://github.com/williamgiare/postmodes . It compares two posterior distributions, p A ​ ( 𝜽 ) p_{A}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) and p B ​ ( 𝜽 ) p_{B}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) , defined over the same set of N N parameters. Starting from their posterior means and covariance matrices, it quantifies the differences between B B and A A by characterizing shifts in the posterior centers, changes in the orientation of the principal degeneracy directions, and variations in the relative constraining power along specific parameter combinations. It also separates changes in the overall scale of the posterior covariance from direction-dependent deformations. The method requires finite second moments and positive-definite covariance matrices, but does not assume Gaussian posterior distributions. 9 9 9 For non-Gaussian posteriors, the resulting diagnostics characterize their second-moment geometry rather than their complete shapes or highest-posterior-density regions. In the concrete application considered here, A A denotes the posterior obtained using the full CMB likelihood, while B B denotes the corresponding posterior obtained using the compressed CMB likelihood. The comparison is based on the posterior mean vectors 𝝁 A \boldsymbol{\mu}_{A} , 𝝁 B \boldsymbol{\mu}_{B} and covariance matrices 𝐂 A \mathbf{C}_{A} , 𝐂 B \mathbf{C}_{B} , extracted directly from the corresponding MCMC chains. In the following, we define the diagnostic quantities used to characterize their agreement and discuss what each of them reveals about the impact of CMB compression on the multidimensional posterior. Additional documentation, worked examples, and validation tests are provided with the PostModes package.

sections.heading: III.2.1 Individual posterior geometry
sections.text: The covariance geometry of the two posteriors is characterized through the principal-component decompositions 𝐂 A = 𝐄 A ​ 𝚲 A ​ 𝐄 A T , 𝐂 B = 𝐄 B ​ 𝚲 B ​ 𝐄 B T , \mathbf{C}_{A}=\mathbf{E}_{A}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{A}\mathbf{E}_{A}^{T},\qquad\mathbf{C}_{B}=\mathbf{E}_{B}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{B}\mathbf{E}_{B}^{T}, (7) where 𝐄 A \mathbf{E}_{A} and 𝐄 B \mathbf{E}_{B} define the principal directions of the corresponding posterior covariances, while the eigenvalues contained in 𝚲 A \mathbf{\Lambda}_{A} and 𝚲 B \mathbf{\Lambda}_{B} determine the variances along those directions. This decomposition provides a first characterization of the parameter combinations that are most and least constrained by the full- and compressed-CMB posterior distributions. Since the resulting eigenvectors depend on the adopted parametrization and units, we do not interpret their individual coefficients as coordinate-independent measures of physical importance.

sections.heading: III.2.4 Relative constraining power: generalized modes
sections.text: To identify the parameter combinations whose uncertainties change most strongly when the full CMB likelihood is replaced by its compressed counterpart, we whiten the covariance of posterior B B with respect to the covariance of posterior A A . We define 𝐂 ~ = 𝐂 A − 1 / 2 𝐂 B 𝐂 A − 1 / 2 . \mathbf{\tilde{C}}=\mathbf{C}_{A}^{-1/2}\,\mathbf{C}_{B}\,\mathbf{C}_{A}^{-1/2}. (14) This transformation maps the covariance of the full-CMB posterior A A to the identity, corresponding to a unit hypersphere in which every direction has unit variance. The matrix 𝐂 ~ \widetilde{\mathbf{C}} then represents the covariance of the compressed-CMB posterior B B in the same coordinates. Deviations of 𝐂 ~ \widetilde{\mathbf{C}} from the identity therefore directly quantify how the compression changes the posterior widths along different parameter combinations. The parameter combinations that diagonalize this relative deformation are obtained from the generalized eigenvalue problem 𝐂 B ​ 𝒗 i = ρ i ​ 𝐂 A ​ 𝒗 i \mathbf{C}_{B}\boldsymbol{v}_{i}=\rho_{i}\mathbf{C}_{A}\boldsymbol{v}_{i} . Defining the corresponding modes as m i = 𝒗 i T ​ ( 𝜽 − 𝝁 A ) m_{i}=\boldsymbol{v}_{i}^{T}(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}) the generalized eigenvalues satisfy ρ i = Var B ⁡ ( m i ) Var A ⁡ ( m i ) . \rho_{i}=\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{B}(m_{i})}{\operatorname{Var}_{A}(m_{i})}. (15) They therefore provide a direct measure of the relative constraining power of the two analyses along each mode, with the following interpretation: • ρ i > 1 \rho_{i}>1 : the posterior B B is broader than the posterior A A along mode m i m_{i} ; • ρ i < 1 \rho_{i}<1 : the posterior B B is tighter than the posterior A A along mode m i m_{i} ; • ρ i = 1 \rho_{i}=1 : the variance along mode m i m_{i} is unchanged between A A and B B . The corresponding ratio of standard deviations is ρ i \sqrt{\rho_{i}} . We further define ρ min ≡ min i ⁡ ρ i , ρ max ≡ max i ⁡ ρ i , \rho_{\min}\equiv\min_{i}\rho_{i},\qquad\rho_{\max}\equiv\max_{i}\rho_{i}, (16) which identify the smallest and largest relative variance ratios across all modes. They therefore quantify the most extreme changes in constraining power induced by the CMB compression.

sections.heading: III.2.5 Isotropic scaling and anisotropic deformation
sections.text: The generalized eigenvalues can be further decomposed into an overall isotropic rescaling of the posterior covariance and a residual anisotropic deformation. We quantify the overall isotropic rescaling of the posterior covariance as α = ( det 𝐂 B det 𝐂 A ) 1 / N = exp ⁡ ( 1 N ​ ∑ i ln ⁡ ρ i ) . \alpha=\left(\frac{\det\mathbf{C}_{B}}{\det\mathbf{C}_{A}}\right)^{1/N}=\exp\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\ln\rho_{i}\right). (17) In the absence of anisotropic deformation, one would have 𝐂 B = α ​ 𝐂 A \mathbf{C}_{B}=\alpha\,\mathbf{C}_{A} , so that α \sqrt{\alpha} gives the common rescaling of the posterior standard deviations. More generally, α \alpha is the geometric mean of the generalized variance ratios ρ i \rho_{i} and captures the overall change in scale independently of direction-dependent distortions. Values α > 1 \alpha>1 correspond to an overall broadening of posterior B B relative to A A , while α < 1 \alpha<1 corresponds to an overall tightening. The case α = 1 \alpha=1 indicates no net isotropic rescaling, although direction-dependent deformations may still be present. The remaining anisotropic deformation is quantified by A aniso = [ 1 N ​ ∑ i ( ln ⁡ ρ i − ln ⁡ α ) 2 ] 1 / 2 . A_{\rm aniso}=\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\left(\ln\rho_{i}-\ln\alpha\right)^{2}\right]^{1/2}. (18) This quantity measures the dispersion of the generalized variance ratios around the isotropic rescaling α \alpha . It vanishes for a purely uniform rescaling, 𝐂 B = α ​ 𝐂 A \mathbf{C}_{B}=\alpha\,\mathbf{C}_{A} , and increases as the relative change in constraining power becomes more direction dependent. Taken together, these diagnostics provide a complementary characterization of how the compressed posterior differs from the full-CMB reference. The SCCD quantifies shifts in the posterior center, the overlap matrix tracks changes in the principal degeneracy directions, and the generalized eigenvalues ρ i \rho_{i} quantify directional changes in constraining power. The parameters α \alpha and A aniso A_{\rm aniso} further separate the overall isotropic rescaling of the posterior covariance from its residual anisotropic deformation.

sections.heading: IV Models
sections.text: In this section, we introduce the cosmological models used to compare the compressed and full CMB likelihoods.

sections.heading: IV.1 Λ \Lambda CDM
sections.text: The standard spatially flat Λ \Lambda CDM model serves as the benchmark cosmology used to calibrate and validate the compressed CMB likelihood. Its background expansion reads E 2 ​ ( a ) = Ω r ​ a − 4 + Ω m ​ a − 3 + Ω Λ , E^{2}(a)=\Omega_{r}\,a^{-4}+\Omega_{m}\,a^{-3}+\Omega_{\Lambda}, (19) with Ω m + Ω r + Ω Λ = 1 \Omega_{m}+\Omega_{r}+\Omega_{\Lambda}=1 . Here, Ω r \Omega_{r} , Ω m \Omega_{m} , and Ω Λ \Omega_{\Lambda} denote the present-day radiation, matter, and cosmological-constant density parameters, respectively. Since the compression is calibrated within Λ \Lambda CDM, this model provides the baseline case in which the compressed likelihood is expected to closely reproduce the constraints obtained from the full CMB analysis.

sections.heading: IV.2 w w CDM
sections.text: The simplest extension of Λ \Lambda CDM considered in this work replaces the cosmological constant with a dark-energy component characterized by a constant EoS parameter, w DE ​ ( a ) = w 0 w_{\rm DE}(a)=w_{0} for all a a . 12 12 12 Various works over the past years have examined constraints on w 0 w_{0} in light of cosmological data. One of the most recent analyses finds w 0 = − 1.013 − 0.043 + 0.038 w_{0}=-1.013^{+0.038}_{-0.043} from a combination of SDSS BAO, PantheonPlus unanchored SN, cosmic chronometers, and Planck PR3 CMB likelihoods, fully consistent with the cosmological-constant scenario [ 109 ] . A later analysis replacing SDSS BAO with DESI measurements finds w 0 = − 1.049 ± 0.024 w_{0}=-1.049\pm 0.024 , approximately 2 ​ σ 2\sigma below the cosmological-constant value [ 246 ] . Its energy density evolves as ρ DE ​ ( a ) = ρ DE , 0 ​ a − 3 ​ ( 1 + w 0 ) \rho_{\rm DE}(a)=\rho_{{\rm DE},0}a^{-3(1+w_{0})} , so that, for a spatially flat Universe, E 2 ​ ( a ) = Ω r ​ a − 4 + Ω m ​ a − 3 + Ω DE ​ a − 3 ​ ( 1 + w 0 ) . E^{2}(a)=\Omega_{r}\,a^{-4}+\Omega_{m}\,a^{-3}+\Omega_{\rm DE}\,a^{-3(1+w_{0})}. (20) The Λ \Lambda CDM limit is recovered for w 0 = − 1 w_{0}=-1 , while w 0 > − 1 w_{0}>-1 and w 0 < − 1 w_{0}<-1 correspond, respectively, to the quintessence-like and phantom regimes. Importantly for our analysis, varying w 0 w_{0} modifies the late-time expansion history while leaving the standard evolution of the matter densities unchanged. The physical matter abundance constrained around recombination therefore retains its usual relation to the present-day matter density, while changes in H ⁡ ( a ) H(a) modify the distance to last scattering and the subsequent growth of structure. At the perturbation level, dark-energy fluctuations and the modified late-time gravitational potentials affect the large-scale CMB anisotropies through the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect and alter the lensing of the primary CMB spectra. The primary acoustic physics at recombination, however, remains essentially unchanged.

sections.heading: IV.3 CPL dynamical dark energy
sections.text: We next consider a time-dependent dark-energy EoS described by the CPL parametrization [ 68 , 191 ] 13 13 13 Several alternative, typically two-parameter, parametrizations of the EoS exist in the literature, see, e.g., Refs. Here w 0 w_{0} denotes the present-day value of the dark-energy EoS, while w a w_{a} controls its evolution with scale factor. 14 14 14 Although the CPL form can be formally interpreted as a first-order expansion of w DE ​ ( a ) w_{\rm DE}(a) around the present epoch, it has also been shown to provide an accurate representation of the observables predicted by a broad class of physical quintessence models [ 191 , 192 , 78 , 190 ] . It can therefore be viewed more generally as a physics-motivated description of the dark-energy phase space spanned by w DE ​ ( a ) w_{\rm DE}(a) and d ​ w DE ​ ( a ) / d ​ ln ⁡ a dw_{\rm DE}(a)/d\ln a [ 193 ] ; see, however, Ref. [ 210 ] . For a recent critical assessment of cosmological constraints on CPL dark energy, see Ref. [ 126 ] . The corresponding dark-energy density evolves as ρ DE ​ ( a ) = ρ DE , 0 ​ a − 3 ​ ( 1 + w 0 + w a ) ​ exp ⁡ [ − 3 ​ w a ​ ( 1 − a ) ] , \rho_{\rm DE}(a)=\rho_{{\rm DE},0}\,a^{-3(1+w_{0}+w_{a})}\exp\left[-3w_{a}(1-a)\right], (21) so that the background expansion is given by E 2 ​ ( a ) = \displaystyle E^{2}(a)={} Ω r ​ a − 4 + Ω m ​ a − 3 \displaystyle\Omega_{r}\,a^{-4}+\Omega_{m}\,a^{-3} (22) + Ω DE ​ a − 3 ​ ( 1 + w 0 + w a ) ​ exp ⁡ [ − 3 ​ w a ​ ( 1 − a ) ] . \displaystyle+\Omega_{\rm DE}\,a^{-3(1+w_{0}+w_{a})}\exp\left[-3w_{a}(1-a)\right]. The Λ \Lambda CDM limit is recovered for ( w 0 , w a ) = ( − 1 , 0 ) (w_{0},w_{a})=(-1,0) , while w a = 0 w_{a}=0 reduces the model to w w CDM. Recent DESI DR2 results show a preference for the region w 0 > − 1 w_{0}>-1 and w a < 0 w_{a}<0 when BAO measurements are combined with CMB and SN data [ 6 ] . 15 15 15 This finding is supported across several dataset combinations and has been shown to be relatively robust to different analysis choices [ 132 ] , although its interpretation and significance remain under debate [ 244 , 77 , 159 , 242 , 270 ] . As in w w CDM, this extension modifies only the dark-energy sector while the standard scaling of the matter densities is preserved and the physical matter abundance constrained around recombination retains its usual relation to its present-day value. At the perturbation level, the evolving dark-energy component also affects the late-time gravitational potentials and the growth of structure, leaving signatures through the ISW effect and the lensing of the primary CMB spectra. These effects remain relatively limited for the smooth dark-energy component considered here because c s , DE 2 = 1 c_{s,\rm DE}^{2}=1 suppresses dark-energy clustering on sub-horizon scales. The acoustic physics responsible for the primary CMB anisotropies at recombination, however, remains essentially unchanged. 16 16 16 When the dark-energy EoS crosses the phantom divide, dark-energy fluctuations are evolved using the parametrized post-Friedmann (PPF) prescription [ 112 , 146 ] , which ensures a regular treatment through w DE = − 1 w_{\rm DE}=-1 .

sections.heading: IV.4 Sign-switching cosmological constant
sections.text: We next consider the so-called Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM model, in which the positive cosmological constant of Λ \Lambda CDM is replaced by a vacuum-energy component that changes sign at a transition redshift z = z † z=z_{\dagger} [ 20 , 17 ] . For z > z † z>z_{\dagger} , the vacuum-energy contribution is negative and corresponds to an anti-de Sitter vacuum, while for z < z † z<z_{\dagger} it becomes positive with the same magnitude, corresponding to a de Sitter vacuum. Defining the corresponding transition scale factor as a † ≡ 1 / ( 1 + z † ) a_{\dagger}\equiv 1/(1+z_{\dagger}) , the background expansion reads E 2 ​ ( a ) = Ω r ​ a − 4 + Ω m ​ a − 3 + Ω Λ s ​ sgn ​ ( a − a † ) , E^{2}(a)=\Omega_{r}\,a^{-4}+\Omega_{m}\,a^{-3}+\Omega_{\Lambda_{\rm s}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(a-a_{\dagger}), (23) where sgn ⁡ ( x ) \mathrm{sgn}(x) denotes the signum function. The Λ \Lambda CDM expansion history is recovered in the limit z † → ∞ z_{\dagger}\rightarrow\infty . The model was originally motivated by the graduated dark-energy scenario [ 12 ] , in which the dark-energy density evolves continuously and can change sign during the late-time expansion. Subsequent analyses showed that cosmological observations favor a relatively rapid transition [ 19 ] , motivating the idealized Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM limit in which the sign change is taken to be abrupt. 17 17 17 Different microphysical realizations of such a phenomenological parametrization have been proposed, ranging from Casimir forces and thin-wall vacuum decay in string-inspired extra-dimensional scenarios [ 26 , 25 , 24 ] , to type-II minimally modified gravity [ 16 , 15 ] and teleparallel f ⁡ ( T ) f(T) gravity [ 13 , 262 ] . Depending on the underlying microphysics, additional degrees of freedom or modified perturbation dynamics may arise. Such effects are model dependent and are not considered in this work. The Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM model has since been extensively studied [ 223 , 26 , 222 , 16 , 25 , 15 , 294 , 24 , 13 , 262 , 261 , 14 , 48 , 49 , 295 , 18 ] , partly because of its ability to mildly alleviate the Hubble tension and the S 8 S_{8} discrepancy for sufficiently low transition redshifts, z † ≲ 2 z_{\dagger}\lesssim 2 [ 20 , 19 , 17 ] . However, like other late-time modifications of the expansion history, Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM remains subject to the general limitations of late-time solutions [ 163 , 167 , 53 , 52 , 236 , 231 , 268 , 225 , 35 , 226 , 243 ] . For the purposes of this work, we use the Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM model as a complementary test of CMB compression. The negative vacuum-energy contribution at z > z † z>z_{\dagger} reduces the expansion rate relative to Λ \Lambda CDM during part of the post-recombination evolution. Preserving the CMB angular acoustic scale then requires a compensating change at lower redshift, which can lead to the larger inferred values of H 0 H_{0} discussed above. As in the w w CDM and CPL cases, the physical matter density continues to scale as ρ m ∝ a − 3 \rho_{m}\propto a^{-3} . Therefore, the physical matter abundance constrained around recombination retains its standard relation to its present-day value, while the primary acoustic physics at recombination remains unchanged. Unlike w w CDM and CPL, however, Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM introduces a much sharper and more localized modification of the late-time expansion. At the perturbation level, on either side of the transition, the vacuum-energy component behaves as a cosmological constant and carries no independent perturbations.

sections.heading: IV.6 Decaying dark matter into dark radiation
sections.text: We then consider a decaying dark-matter scenario in which a cold, pressureless dark-matter component (hereafter denoted by the subscript dcdm) decays into invisible relativistic particles that behave as dark-radiation (hereafter denoted by the subscript dr) [ 33 , 230 ] . 19 19 19 For interesting studies of decaying dark matter into invisible relativistic particles and dark radiation, see, e.g., Refs. Consequently, the choice c s , dm 2 = 0 c_{s,\rm dm}^{2}=0 describes an intrinsically non-adiabatic dark-matter fluid whenever w dm , 0 ≠ 0 w_{\rm dm,0}\neq 0 . This eliminates pressure-gradient support and allows the dark-matter component to remain clustering despite its non-zero background EoS. In synchronous gauge, the corresponding Euler equation takes the standard form θ dm ′ = − ℋ ​ θ dm . \theta_{\rm dm}^{\prime}=-\mathcal{H}\theta_{\rm dm}. (44) The usual gauge choice comoving with dark matter, θ dm = 0 \theta_{\rm dm}=0 , is therefore preserved. The density contrast instead obeys δ dm ′ = − 1 + w dm , 0 2 ​ h ′ + 3 ​ ℋ ​ w dm , 0 ​ δ dm . \delta_{\rm dm}^{\prime}=-\frac{1+w_{\rm dm,0}}{2}h^{\prime}+3\mathcal{H}w_{\rm dm,0}\,\delta_{\rm dm}. (45) The perturbations therefore differ from those of standard CDM even though the rest-frame sound speed vanishes. For the purposes of this work, Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM provides a second direct test of CMB compression in a scenario where the dark-matter sector is modified while dark energy remains a cosmological constant. The main difference with the decaying-dark-matter scenario is that, while the effects of dark-matter decay become most relevant at late times, in Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM the dark-matter evolution differs from the standard scaling throughout the entire cosmological history.

sections.heading: V Results
sections.text: We now present the cosmological constraints obtained using the datasets and methodology described in Sec. III for the models introduced in Sec. IV . For each model, we first compare the marginalized constraints and two-dimensional posterior distributions obtained from dataset A A (i.e., full Planck-CMB+DESI+PantheonPlus) and dataset B B (i.e., compressed Planck-CMB+DESI+PantheonPlus). We then complement this comparison with the multidimensional posterior diagnostics introduced in Sec. III . Throughout this section, we focus exclusively on the quantitative agreement or disagreement between the two posterior distributions. Readers primarily interested in the overall pattern emerging from the model-by-model analysis may proceed directly to Sec. V.8 . The physical origin of this pattern and its broader implications are instead discussed in Sec. VI . The marginalized parameter constraints obtained from A A and B B for the different cosmological models are reported in Tables 1 – 7 , together with the corresponding one- and two-dimensional posterior distributions shown in Figures 1 – 7 . Unless otherwise stated, marginalized constraints are quoted at 68 % 68\% confidence level (CL), while one-tail bounds are given at 95 % 95\% CL. The multidimensional comparison of the posterior distributions obtained with PostModes is instead summarized in Table 8 . Figure 8 additionally shows the eigenvector-overlap matrices for a few particularly instructive cases, which are discussed in the corresponding subsections below.

sections.heading: V.8 Overall pattern
sections.text: The results above reveal a clear separation in the performance of the compressed likelihood across the models considered. For Λ \Lambda CDM, w w CDM, CPL, and Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM, the compressed likelihood reproduces both the marginalized constraints and the multidimensional posterior geometry with high accuracy. In all four cases, the multidimensional diagnostics remain close to their reference values, with α \sqrt{\alpha} differing from unity by less than ∼ 1 % \sim 1\% , A aniso ≲ 0.06 A_{\rm aniso}\lesssim 0.06 , and the extrema of ρ i \sqrt{\rho_{i}} staying within ∼ 4 % \sim 4\% of unity. IDE, DCDMDR and Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM instead show substantially larger differences between A A and B B . Their center separations increase to S CC ≃ 0.98 S_{\rm CC}\simeq 0.98 – 2.12 2.12 , while A aniso ≃ 1.38 A_{\rm aniso}\simeq 1.38 – 1.87 1.87 . In each case, at least one generalized mode is substantially narrower in the compressed posterior, with ρ min ≃ 0.11 \sqrt{\rho_{\min}}\simeq 0.11 – 0.25 0.25 , while other directions are much less affected or can become broader. These geometric differences are reflected in substantial changes in the marginalized constraints and correlations involving the additional model parameters. The origin of this systematic pattern and its implications for the validity of CMB compression are discussed in the following section.

The results discussed in the previous section reveal a clear separation in the performance of the compressed CMB likelihood. In Λ \Lambda CDM, w w CDM, CPL, and Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM, the two prescriptions yield nearly identical marginalized constraints and multidimensional posterior geometries. Conversely, substantial differences emerge for IDE, DCDMDR, and Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM. Since models introducing new physics that acts predominantly at late times appear on both sides of this separation, a simple distinction between early- and late-time modifications is not sufficient to determine whether the compression scheme remains reliable. A more informative distinction is that all three models showing a breakdown directly modify the evolution of the dark-matter sector. Whenever the standard evolution of the matter components is preserved (i.e., ρ b ∝ a − 3 \rho_{b}\propto a^{-3} and ρ dm ∝ a − 3 \rho_{\rm dm}\propto a^{-3} ), the present-day physical matter density ω m = ω b + ω dm + ω ν \omega_{m}=\omega_{b}+\omega_{\rm dm}+\omega_{\nu} is a natural compression variable because, for a fixed neutrino sector, it uniquely determines the corresponding matter abundance around recombination. This one-to-one mapping is preserved in Λ \Lambda CDM, w w CDM, CPL, and Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM. By contrast, in IDE, DCDMDR, and Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM this mapping is broken because the dark-matter density evolves non-standardly. In these models, fixing the same present-day value of ω m \omega_{m} implies a different dark-matter abundance (and hence a different total matter abundance) at recombination. A different matter abundance at recombination, in turn, can substantially modify the CMB angular power spectra by shifting the epoch of matter-radiation equality and changing the depth and evolution of the gravitational potentials that drive the acoustic oscillations. Consequently, the same present-day value of ω m \omega_{m} no longer corresponds to the same physical conditions at recombination as in models that preserve the standard evolution of the matter components. To test directly this interpretation, we proceed in three steps. We first quantify how strongly the standard mapping between the present-day and earlier dark-matter abundances is violated in the three models for which the compression fails. We then examine how this altered mapping changes the dark-matter abundance relevant at recombination and how this is reflected in the full and compressed CMB posteriors. Finally, we discuss the main caveats surrounding perturbative effects that are not captured by the background mapping alone.

sections.heading: VI.0.1 Quantifying the breakdown of the dark-matter scaling
sections.text: To quantify departures from the standard evolution of the dark-matter component, we define ℳ dm ​ ( z ) ≡ ρ dm ​ ( z ) ρ dm , 0 ​ ( 1 + z ) 3 . {\cal M}_{\rm dm}(z)\equiv\frac{\rho_{\rm dm}(z)}{\rho_{{\rm dm},0}(1+z)^{3}}. For stable pressureless dark matter, ℳ dm ​ ( z ) = 1 {\cal M}_{\rm dm}(z)=1 at all redshifts. More generally, this quantity provides two complementary pieces of information. First, if the dark-matter density scales as ρ dm ∝ ( 1 + z ) 3 \rho_{\rm dm}\propto(1+z)^{3} , then ℳ dm ​ ( z ) {\cal M}_{\rm dm}(z) is constant. Its redshift dependence therefore directly signals departures from the standard dark-matter redshift evolution. Second, its absolute value quantifies the cumulative mismatch between the actual dark-matter abundance at a given redshift and that obtained by extrapolating the present-day abundance using the standard relation ρ dm ∝ ( 1 + z ) 3 \rho_{\rm dm}\propto(1+z)^{3} . In particular, ℳ dm > 1 {\cal M}_{\rm dm}>1 means that the standard extrapolation underestimates the actual dark-matter abundance at a given redshift, whereas ℳ dm < 1 {\cal M}_{\rm dm}<1 means that it overestimates it. We reconstruct ℳ dm ​ ( z ) {\cal M}_{\rm dm}(z) from the posterior samples of A A and B B for the three models in which the compression shows a significant breakdown, over a redshift range extending to the epochs relevant to the CMB. The resulting central curves and 68 % 68\% credible regions are shown in Figure 9 . For IDE, the evolution of ℳ dm ​ ( z ) {\cal M}_{\rm dm}(z) follows directly from the conservation equation. At late times, the interaction modifies the relation between the present-day dark-matter density and its value in the past, see Eq. ( 29 ). At sufficiently high redshift, however, ρ DE / ρ dm \rho_{\rm DE}/\rho_{\rm dm} becomes small and the interaction term becomes negligible relative to the standard dilution term. The dark matter therefore approaches the standard scaling ρ dm ∝ ( 1 + z ) 3 \rho_{\rm dm}\propto(1+z)^{3} , causing ℳ dm ​ ( z ) {\cal M}_{\rm dm}(z) to approach a constant value, as seen in Figure 9 . Importantly, this asymptotic value is not equal to unity. Thus, although the dark matter recovers the standard redshift scaling at high redshift, its abundance remains offset from the standard backward extrapolation of the present-day density. In particular, extrapolating the present-day density backward according to that scaling would underestimate the actual dark-matter abundance at recombination. As shown in the middle panel of Figure 9 , DCDMDR exhibits the same qualitative behavior of ℳ dcdm ​ ( z ) {\cal M}_{\rm dcdm}(z) , but for a different physical reason. The density of the decaying dark-matter component evolves according to Eq. ( 36 ). Going backward in time, the expansion rate becomes increasingly large relative to the fixed physical decay rate, so that the fractional effect of the decay over a Hubble time becomes progressively smaller. The decaying dark matter therefore approaches the standard scaling ρ dcdm ∝ ( 1 + z ) 3 \rho_{\rm dcdm}\propto(1+z)^{3} , causing ℳ dcdm ​ ( z ) {\cal M}_{\rm dcdm}(z) to approach a constant value. As in IDE, however, this asymptotic value is not equal to unity. Extrapolating the present-day density backward according to the standard scaling would therefore underestimate the actual abundance of the decaying dark-matter component at recombination. The behavior is qualitatively different for Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM, as shown in the right panel of Figure 9 . In this case, the dark-matter density evolves according to Eq. ( 43 ), and therefore ℳ dm ​ ( z ) = ( 1 + z ) 3 ​ w dm , 0 {\cal M}_{\rm dm}(z)=(1+z)^{3w_{\rm dm,0}} . Unlike IDE and DCDMDR, as long as w dm , 0 ≠ 0 w_{\rm dm,0}\neq 0 , the dark-matter density does not recover the standard ( 1 + z ) 3 (1+z)^{3} scaling and ℳ dm ​ ( z ) {\cal M}_{\rm dm}(z) does not approach a nonzero constant value at high redshift. Instead, the departure from the standard mapping grows continuously with redshift. The direction of this departure depends on the sign of the dark-matter EoS: for w dm , 0 > 0 w_{\rm dm,0}>0 , ℳ dm > 1 {\cal M}_{\rm dm}>1 and the standard backward extrapolation underestimates the actual dark-matter abundance, whereas for w dm , 0 < 0 w_{\rm dm,0}<0 , ℳ dm < 1 {\cal M}_{\rm dm}<1 and it overestimates it. In either case, the mismatch increases with redshift and can become substantial at the characteristic redshifts probed by the CMB. This persistent accumulation of the mismatch provides a natural explanation for why Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM shows the most pronounced breakdown of the compressed likelihood among the models considered.

sections.heading: VI.0.3 Caveats surrounding cosmological perturbations
sections.text: The background-level mapping identified above does not exhaust the information carried by the full CMB likelihood. Importantly, IDE, DCDMDR, and Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM also modify the evolution of cosmological perturbations, which can introduce further model-dependent changes in the CMB spectra and in the corresponding parameter degeneracies. The role of perturbations should therefore be distinguished according to three different cases. • If a model modifies both the dark-matter background evolution and its perturbations, as in IDE, DCDMDR, and Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM, the breakdown of the background mapping discussed here is sufficient to invalidate the standard compressed likelihood. Perturbative effects can add further model-dependent information to the CMB anisotropies and posterior degeneracies that is not retained by the compression. However, they cannot restore the background relation on which the compression is based. • If the standard dark-matter background evolution is preserved and the background modification is confined to late-time dark energy, the situation is different. For the models considered here, namely w w CDM, CPL, and Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM, we find that the compression reproduces the full-CMB constraints well. This result should nevertheless be interpreted with the caveat that more general dark-energy models may exhibit significant perturbative effects that are not captured by the geometric compression. For example, a sufficiently large modification of the late-time ISW contribution could introduce additional information even if the background mapping and acoustic-scale geometry remain well preserved. The perturbation sector should therefore be checked separately before extending the agreement found here to more general dark-energy models. • Finally, if the new physics modifies only cosmological perturbations while leaving the background unchanged, a CMB compression based only on background and acoustic-scale quantities is by construction insensitive to the relevant new information. In this case, the compressed likelihood cannot be expected to provide meaningful constraints on the additional physics.

sections.heading: VII Conclusions
sections.text: In this work, we have investigated when compressed CMB likelihoods can be reliably used beyond Λ \Lambda CDM, why they fail for some classes of models, and how such failures propagate into the inferred cosmological constraints. To address these questions, we considered a broad set of theoretical extensions that modify different sectors and epochs of the cosmological model. We considered late-time dark-energy modifications with a constant EoS ( w w CDM), smooth dynamical evolution (CPL), and an abrupt transition ( Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM). We also considered models that modify the dark-matter evolution predominantly at late times, either through an interaction with dark energy (IDE) or through decay into dark radiation (DCDMDR). Finally, we considered Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM, in which the dark-matter EoS is allowed to deviate from zero, modifying its redshift evolution throughout the entire cosmological history. For each model, we compared the constraints obtained from two datasets. Dataset A A combines the full Planck-CMB likelihood with DESI and PantheonPlus data. Dataset B B replaces the full CMB likelihood with the compressed CMB likelihood calibrated from the Λ \Lambda CDM CMB-only analysis, keeping the DESI and PantheonPlus data unchanged. We compared both the marginalized parameter constraints and the full multidimensional posterior geometry using PostModes , a package developed in this work to quantify differences between high-dimensional posterior distributions. We formulate concrete criteria for when , why , and how the CMB compression fails. • When: The relevant distinction is not whether the new physics acts at early or late times, but whether the model preserves the physical relations assumed by the compressed variables. Three cases should be distinguished. First , if a model modifies the background evolution of dark matter, as in IDE, DCDMDR, and Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM, the standard relation between the present-day matter density and the dark-matter abundance relevant to the CMB is no longer preserved. The background-level violation is already sufficient to invalidate the standard compressed likelihood. Perturbative effects may introduce additional model-dependent differences, but they cannot restore the background mapping on which the compression was calibrated. Second , if the standard dark-matter evolution is preserved and the background modification is confined to the late-time dark-energy sector, the compression can remain reliable, as we find for w w CDM, CPL, and Λ s \Lambda_{\rm s} CDM. Nevertheless, this result is not a general guarantee for arbitrary dark-energy models. Significant perturbative effects, for example a large modification of the late-time ISW contribution, could carry CMB information that is not retained by the compressed likelihood and should therefore be checked case by case. Third , if the new physics enters only through cosmological perturbations while leaving the background unchanged, a compression based on background and geometric quantities alone is by construction insensitive to the relevant new information and cannot be expected to constrain that physics. • Why: The CMB spectra, and therefore the full CMB likelihood, are primarily sensitive to the matter abundance at the epochs relevant to the formation of the primary CMB anisotropies, particularly matter-radiation equality and recombination. When the standard matter evolution is preserved, the present-day physical matter density uniquely determines the corresponding abundance at the redshifts probed by the CMB. This one-to-one relation is what makes ω m \omega_{m} a useful compression variable. If the dark-matter evolution is modified, however, this mapping can fail in two qualitatively different ways. First, the dark matter may recover the standard ( 1 + z ) 3 (1+z)^{3} scaling at high redshift while retaining a different normalization, so that the present-day density still extrapolates to the wrong abundance around recombination. This happens in IDE and DCDMDR, where the new physics modifies the dark-matter evolution predominantly at late times. Second, the redshift scaling itself may remain non-standard at all relevant redshifts. This occurs in Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM, where the dark-matter EoS is allowed to deviate from zero and modifies its scaling throughout the cosmological evolution. In either case, preserving the matter abundance at the epochs probed by the CMB requires adjusting the present-day dark-matter density ω dm \omega_{\rm dm} accordingly. For fixed baryon and neutrino sectors, this necessarily shifts the present-day matter density ω m \omega_{m} as well. The full CMB likelihood evaluates the actual spectra for each parameter combination and can therefore accommodate such shifts when changes in the additional model parameter keep the CMB spectra nearly unchanged. The compressed likelihood instead constrains ω m \omega_{m} using the distribution calibrated in Λ \Lambda CDM. It therefore penalizes shifts in the present-day dark-matter density through the corresponding change in ω m \omega_{m} , even along degeneracy directions that leave the CMB spectra nearly unchanged. As a result, degeneracy directions present in the full CMB likelihood are lost or distorted in the compressed analysis. • How: An incorrect use of the CMB compression can deform the geometry of the multidimensional posterior and distort the marginalized cosmological constraints. We show that this can occur in several qualitatively different ways. The compression can shift the posterior center, compress or broaden different directions by very different amounts, alter the relative ordering of principal modes, and, in more severe cases, rotate and mix the eigendirections themselves. The models studied here provide concrete examples of these possibilities. In IDE, the dominant effect is a strongly anisotropic deformation associated with the altered relation between ξ \xi and ω dm \omega_{\rm dm} . In DCDMDR, the compression changes the relative widths of nearly preserved principal directions enough to reorder the modes, with the conversion of dark matter into dark radiation further complicating the posterior geometry. In Λ ​ w \Lambda w DM, where the full dark-matter density history is modified, the failure extends beyond anisotropic changes in the posterior widths and produces genuine mixing and reorientation of the principal eigendirections. When these multidimensional distortions are projected onto the one- and two-dimensional marginalized constraints normally reported in cosmological analyses, they can appear as shifted central values or substantially tightened or weakened bounds. The resulting differences can be very large. For example, the constraint on ξ \xi in IDE differs by nearly an order of magnitude, while the upper bound on Γ dcdm \Gamma_{\rm dcdm} in DCDMDR changes by about a factor of four. It is also important to stress that agreement in a well-measured quantity such as the acoustic scale is not sufficient to demonstrate that the full posterior geometry has been preserved. In conclusion, our results identify a restricted regime in which compressed CMB likelihoods can be used reliably: late-time dark-energy extensions that preserve the standard dark-matter background evolution and do not introduce significant additional perturbative effects. Outside this regime, the burden of proof should be reversed: the full CMB likelihood should be the default, and the compressed likelihood should be used only after its validity has been explicitly demonstrated for the model under consideration. sections.heading: A.2 Dependence on the compression dimensionality
sections.text: We next test whether the failure of the compressed likelihood can be avoided by reducing the dimensionality of the compression. We compare it with datasets A A and B B , defined as in the main analysis. Figure 12 and Table 9 therefore allow us to isolate the effect of reducing the dimensionality of the CMB compression. Reducing the compression to two dimensions does not recover the full-CMB constraints. Instead, the nature of the disagreement changes. While the 3 × 3 3\times 3 compression strongly restricts the IDE degeneracy, removing ω m \omega_{m} discards a substantial amount of CMB information and produces much broader constraints. For example, the full-CMB analysis gives ξ > − 0.124 \xi>-0.124 , compared with ξ > − 0.0150 \xi>-0.0150 for the 3 × 3 3\times 3 compression and ξ > − 0.444 \xi>-0.444 for the 2 × 2 2\times 2 compression. The 2 × 2 2\times 2 compression also produces different correlations among the cosmological parameters, so that the much broader posterior does not simply encompass the full-CMB result. As visible in Figure 12 , the overlap with the full-CMB posterior remains limited in several projections despite the substantially larger uncertainties. The failure of the compressed likelihood is therefore not specific to the inclusion of ω m \omega_{m} as a third compressed parameter. Removing this information does not reconstruct the full likelihood, but instead leads to a different loss of CMB information and a different posterior geometry. We have verified the same behavior for all the models in which the full and compressed CMB likelihoods lead to discrepant constraints in the main analysis.

We derive our conclusions by exploring a broad set of models that modify different aspects of the cosmological evolution, including late-time dark-energy dynamics, non-standard late-time dark-matter evolution through interactions or decay, and dark-matter models with persistently non-standard redshift evolution. For each case, we compare the results obtained from data combinations based on the full Planck-CMB likelihood with their counterparts based on a compressed CMB likelihood calibrated in Λ \Lambda CDM. We find that the compression remains accurate for late-time dark-energy extensions that preserve the dark-matter background evolution and do not introduce significant additional perturbative effects. By contrast, modifying the dark-matter evolution breaks the mapping between the present-day matter density and the matter density at the epochs relevant to the CMB, causing the compressed constraints to fail even when the modification acts exclusively at late times. In these cases, the compressed likelihood can drastically alter the geometry of the multidimensional posterior distributions, shifting their centers, producing strongly anisotropic deformations, reordering principal modes, and generating genuine mixing and rotation of their eigendirections. These multidimensional distortions propagate into substantially incorrect marginalized constraints on cosmological parameters, with differences between the full and compressed analyses reaching nearly an order of magnitude in some of the cases studied here. I Introduction Over more than two decades, full-sky satellite missions such as WMAP [ 39 , 140 ] and Planck [ 9 , 11 ] , complemented by the higher angular resolution of ground-based experiments such as the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) [ 234 , 202 , 197 ] and the South Pole Telescope (SPT) [ 123 , 56 ] , have established the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation as one of the most powerful and precise probes in modern cosmology. The increasing precision of CMB measurements has progressively tightened constraints on cosmological parameters and models of new physics, while confirming the excellent agreement of the observed anisotropies with the standard Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology [ 11 , 202 , 56 ] . At the same time, however, persistent tensions within Λ \Lambda CDM, including the Hubble tension [ 276 , 93 , 89 , 227 , 249 , 252 , 4 , 96 , 158 , 131 , 144 , 277 , 86 , 104 , 94 , 54 ] and the preference for dynamical dark energy recently emerging from DESI analyses [ 6 , 196 ] , 1 1 1 For a non-exhaustive selection of discussions surrounding this preference, see, e.g. [ 79 , 255 , 199 , 125 , 283 , 307 , 265 , 60 , 224 , 105 , 41 , 29 , 185 , 237 , 127 , 235 , 304 , 154 , 240 , 132 , 126 , 103 , 161 , 241 , 248 , 290 , 247 , 263 , 65 , 66 , 217 , 183 , 174 , 113 , 268 , 260 , 55 , 138 , 67 , 70 , 71 , 72 , 151 , 73 , 133 , 150 , 209 , 297 , 97 , 81 , 160 , 184 , 129 , 182 , 238 , 30 ] . have motivated growing interest in alternative models and physical mechanisms beyond the standard cosmological paradigm. 2 2 2 The significance of the so-called S 8 S_{8} tension [ 92 , 85 , 213 , 23 , 250 , 32 , 31 , 156 , 100 , 2 , 272 , 139 , 82 , 64 , 162 , 111 , 137 , 99 , 1 , 291 , 3 ] is milder and less clear-cut. The KiDS-Legacy reanalysis reported values of S 8 S_{8} in good agreement with Planck [ 291 ] , whereas the Dark Energy Survey Year 6 (DES-Y6) results still find a mild mismatch with CMB constraints at ∼ 2.6 \sim 2.6 – 2.8 ​ σ 2.8\sigma [ 3 ] . Since any such mechanism must preserve the level of agreement with CMB data set by Λ \Lambda CDM, confronting models of new physics with CMB observations is more important and timely than ever. However indispensable in practice, testing models of new physics against CMB data has two important limitations. First, it is computationally expensive and inconvenient for efficient scans across large model spaces. Second, it is not easily applicable to models for which the evolution of linear perturbations is either technically and computationally demanding (as often occurs in modified-gravity theories [ 76 , 166 ] ) or not well defined (as in some purely phenomenological models). These limitations have motivated the development of compression schemes , which summarize the information contained in the full CMB power spectrum in a limited number of parameters [ 101 ] . The most notable example is given by the so-called shift parameters ( ℓ a \ell_{a} , R R ), which were first introduced with the aim of exploring cosmic acceleration and the landscape of dark energy models [ 101 , 286 , 287 ] . R ≡ Ω m ​ H 0 2 ​ D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) R\equiv\sqrt{\Omega_{m}H_{0}^{2}}D_{M}(z_{\star}) represents the scaled angular diameter distance to the last-scattering surface, while ℓ a ≡ π ​ D M ​ ( z ⋆ ) / r s ⋆ \ell_{a}\equiv\pi D_{M}(z_{\star})/r_{s}^{\star} defines the multipole corresponding to the characteristic angular scale subtended by the sound horizon at photon decoupling. In Refs. [ 287 , 288 ] it was subsequently shown that combining the shift parameters with the physical baryon density ω b = Ω b ​ h 2 \omega_{b}=\Omega_{b}h^{2} (and possibly the inflationary spectral index n s n_{s} ) provides a compact summary of the CMB information relevant for cosmological parameter constraints. This set of quantities is commonly referred to as the CMB distance priors . 3 3 3 Other methods to compress CMB information have also been explored. For example, in Ref. [ 233 ] the authors applied the Massively Optimized Parameter Estimation and Data compression to the Planck-2015 temperature likelihood and showed that the standard Λ \Lambda CDM cosmological parameter constraints can be derived from a compressed likelihood of just six Gaussian-distributed data points. More recently, Ref. [ 21 ] explored self-supervised machine-learning techniques for data compression and cosmological inference. Despite being among the least model-dependent quantities that can be extracted from the CMB, the shift parameters are not direct observables. Quantities such as ℓ a \ell_{a} and R R are inferred from the observed temperature and polarization power spectra within a fiducial cosmological model, typically Λ \Lambda CDM [ 287 , 205 , 288 ] . Their values and correlations therefore depend on how the fiducial model relates cosmological parameters to the observed CMB features [ 310 ] . Using the resulting compressed likelihood to constrain a different cosmology implicitly assumes that the relevant CMB physics, and hence this mapping, remains sufficiently unchanged [ 205 , 310 ] . A commonly adopted working criterion is to distinguish between modifications occurring before and after recombination. Late-time models are generally expected to be more reliable in this respect, since they leave the physics responsible for the primary CMB anisotropies essentially unchanged [ 287 , 205 , 310 ] . By contrast, pre-recombination new physics can modify the acoustic physics itself and therefore invalidate a compression calibrated within Λ \Lambda CDM [ 253 , 310 ] . A number of studies have therefore assessed the validity and regime of applicability of compressed CMB information beyond the fiducial Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology. Initial studies tested the robustness of the shift parameters against relatively simple departures from flat Λ \Lambda CDM [ 287 , 205 , 288 ] , while later analyses extended these tests to models involving dynamical dark energy, massive neutrinos, additional relativistic degrees of freedom, spatial curvature, and modifications of the primordial power spectrum [ 310 ] . More recently, the compressed likelihood CMBComp [ 264 ] has addressed this model dependence more systematically by constructing compression schemes tailored to specific classes of cosmological models. 4 4 4 For instance, the ν ​ Λ \nu\Lambda CDM model is described by the four-parameter compression ( ℓ a , R , ω b , ω c ) (\ell_{a},R,\omega_{b},\omega_{c}) , calibrated specifically within the corresponding model space. Our work extends these robustness tests with the broader goal of identifying the physical conditions under which compressed CMB information can be reliably used to test models of new physics. In particular, we investigate which properties of a cosmological model determine whether compressed CMB information remains reliable, focusing on the physical sector affected by the new dynamics and on which pieces of CMB information are consequently modified. To this end, we consider a set of phenomenologically motivated models proposed in connection with concrete challenges to the standard cosmological paradigm and use them as representative test cases to isolate qualitatively different departures from the physics underlying the CMB compression. Taking Λ \Lambda CDM as our benchmark scenario, we first extend it by introducing a constant dark-energy equation of state (EoS) w DE w_{\rm DE} . We then consider the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder (CPL) parametrization of dynamical dark energy [ 68 , 191 ] and a sign-switching cosmological constant [ 20 ] . These three models modify the late-time dark-energy background while leaving the standard scaling of the matter densities unchanged. We then turn to interacting dark-energy (IDE) models, where energy exchange within the dark sector alters the dynamics of both dark energy and dark matter [ 46 , 279 ] , and consequently the relation between the dark-matter abundance constrained by the CMB at recombination and its present-day value. Finally, we consider two complementary scenarios in which the departure from Λ \Lambda CDM is confined to the dark-matter sector: decaying dark matter [ 33 , 230 ] and dark matter with a nonzero EoS [ 165 ] . In the former, the dark-matter evolution is modified predominantly at late times, while in the latter the standard scaling ρ dm ∝ a − 3 \rho_{\rm dm}\propto a^{-3} is modified throughout the cosmological evolution. Together, these models allow us to test whether the validity of the CMB compression depends not simply on when the new physics becomes relevant, but on how it modifies the relation between the dark-matter abundance probed by the CMB and its present-day value. We find a clear qualitative distinction depending on the physical sector affected by the new dynamics. The compression remains remarkably robust for models in which the departure from Λ \Lambda CDM is confined to the late-time dark-energy sector and the standard evolution of the matter densities is preserved. By contrast, when the dark-matter sector acquires a non-standard evolution, the compressed likelihood fails to reproduce the constraints obtained from the full CMB temperature and polarization spectra. In these cases, the compressed likelihood can distort the multidimensional geometry of the posterior distributions, ultimately leading to marginalized constraints that in some cases differ by nearly an order of magnitude from those obtained with the full CMB likelihood. We trace this breakdown primarily to the failure of the usual mapping between the dark-matter abundance constrained by the CMB around recombination and its present-day value. In addition, compressing the full spectra into a small number of background quantities can discard perturbation-level information that becomes relevant when the dark-matter sector is modified. Our results therefore show that the validity of compressed CMB information is determined not simply by when new physics becomes active, but also by which physical sector it affects and whether the relations implicitly assumed by the compression remain valid. The paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II we review the compression scheme adopted in our analysis. In Sec. III we discuss the datasets and methodology used to obtain our results, together with the diagnostic tools developed to perform a detailed comparison of the posterior distributions. In Sec. IV we introduce the models against which we test the CMB compression. We present the results in Sec. V . A critical discussion of our findings and their implications follows in Sec. VI . Finally, we present our conclusions in Sec. VII . Additional tests of the robustness of our main conclusions against different compression choices and dataset combinations are presented in Appendix A . II CMB compression In this section, we give a brief introduction to the shift parameters ( R , ℓ a ) (R,\ell_{a}) , which together with the physical baryon density ω b \omega_{b} constitute the CMB distance priors. We then describe their relation to the compression scheme adopted in this paper. The shift parameters R R and ℓ a \ell_{a} capture the dominant geometrical information encoded in the CMB, but an accurate compression must also retain the physical quantities that determine the acoustic structure at recombination. This role is naturally played by the physical baryon density ω b \omega_{b} . Its value directly affects the sound speed of the photon-baryon fluid, the sound horizon, and the relative heights and structure of the acoustic peaks in the CMB spectra. Together, these effects tightly constrain ω b \omega_{b} and generate correlations with the shift parameters that must be preserved in the compression scheme. A notable example is the scalar spectral index, n s n_{s} , whose inclusion becomes relevant when using observables sensitive to the shape of the matter power spectrum [ 205 ] . Since in our analysis BAO measurements are used only as geometrical probes, we do not retain n s n_{s} as an additional compression parameter [ 205 ] . For our purposes, however, the adopted parametrization offers a more transparent physical interpretation by separating the geometrical information carried by the angular acoustic scale from that associated with the physical matter densities. Under standard pre-recombination physics and for fixed radiation and neutrino sectors, the sound horizon r s ⋆ r_{s}^{\star} is determined by the physical densities ω m \omega_{m} and ω b \omega_{b} .
