The two parameters therefore share the same dependence on the distance to last scattering. Replacing R R with ω m \omega_{m} removes this common geometrical dependence and makes the separation between geometry and physical densities explicit. This separation becomes particularly informative when the evolution of the matter sector itself is modified. For completeness, in Appendix A.1 we explicitly verify the equivalence between the two formulations of the CMB distance priors. III dataset and methodology In this section, we describe the datasets and methodology adopted in our analysis. We first summarize the numerical implementation and statistical framework used for cosmological parameter inference. We then describe the tailored geometric posterior analysis developed to quantify the differences between the full and compressed CMB constraints, together with its numerical implementation. III.1 Datasets and standard parameter inference We perform a systematic comparison of cosmological constraints obtained using the full and compressed CMB likelihoods across a set of representative models chosen to isolate qualitatively different departures from Λ \Lambda CDM and identify the physical properties that determine the validity of the CMB compression. Theoretical predictions are computed using the Boltzmann solver CLASS [ 44 , 175 ] . We use the standard public implementation for Λ \Lambda CDM and for scenarios already supported by the code, together with dedicated modified versions for the non-standard dark-energy and dark-matter models introduced in Sec. IV . These implementations consistently evolve the background cosmology and, whenever required for the full-CMB analysis, the associated linear perturbations. For each model, we run parallel Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses using Cobaya [ 271 ] . The chains are evolved until convergence according to the Gelman-Rubin criterion [ 124 ] , requiring R − 1 < 0.01 R-1<0.01 , and subsequently post-processed using GetDist [ 179 ] to derive marginalized parameter constraints and posterior distributions. We further analyze the multidimensional geometry of the posterior distributions using the PostModes package described in the following subsection. The full- and compressed-CMB analyses use the same cosmological parameters, prior distributions, and observational datasets. They differ only in the treatment of the CMB information. In one case, we use the full Planck temperature and polarization likelihood, while in the other we replace it with the compressed likelihood introduced in Sec. II . The observational datasets and likelihoods entering these analyses are the following: • Full Planck-CMB : Our full CMB likelihood is based on the Planck 2018 data [ 10 , 11 ] and combines the low- ℓ \ell temperature Commander likelihood, the low- ℓ \ell E-mode polarization SimAll likelihood, and the high- ℓ \ell Plik TT, TE, and EE likelihood [ 10 ] . We do not include the CMB lensing-reconstruction likelihood because our goal is to compare the information encoded in the primary CMB spectra with that retained by their compression. Including lensing reconstruction would add extra late-time information on structure growth that is not encoded in the compressed likelihood. Gravitational-lensing effects on the primary TT, TE, and EE spectra are nevertheless consistently included. • Compressed Planck-CMB : We perform an MCMC analysis of Λ \Lambda CDM using exclusively the Planck 2018 temperature and polarization data listed above. From the resulting MCMC chains, following the parametrization introduced in Sec. Throughout this work, we denote by • A A : the posterior and marginalized constraints obtained from the full Planck-CMB likelihood combined with DESI BAO and PantheonPlus SN; • B B : the posterior and marginalized constraints obtained from the compressed Planck-CMB likelihood combined with DESI BAO and PantheonPlus SN. III.2 Posterior eigenmode analysis To characterize more systematically the differences between the full and compressed CMB constraints, we complement the standard comparison of marginalized constraints on cosmological parameters with a broader geometric analysis of the corresponding multidimensional posteriors. To this end we develop the PostModes package. 8 8 8 Available at https://github.com/williamgiare/postmodes . It compares two posterior distributions, p A ​ ( 𝜽 ) p_{A}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) and p B ​ ( 𝜽 ) p_{B}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) , defined over the same set of N N parameters. Starting from their posterior means and covariance matrices, it quantifies the differences between B B and A A by characterizing shifts in the posterior centers, changes in the orientation of the principal degeneracy directions, and variations in the relative constraining power along specific parameter combinations. It also separates changes in the overall scale of the posterior covariance from direction-dependent deformations. The method requires finite second moments and positive-definite covariance matrices, but does not assume Gaussian posterior distributions. 9 9 9 For non-Gaussian posteriors, the resulting diagnostics characterize their second-moment geometry rather than their complete shapes or highest-posterior-density regions. In the concrete application considered here, A A denotes the posterior obtained using the full CMB likelihood, while B B denotes the corresponding posterior obtained using the compressed CMB likelihood. The comparison is based on the posterior mean vectors 𝝁 A \boldsymbol{\mu}_{A} , 𝝁 B \boldsymbol{\mu}_{B} and covariance matrices 𝐂 A \mathbf{C}_{A} , 𝐂 B \mathbf{C}_{B} , extracted directly from the corresponding MCMC chains.
